headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. headlines.title: 49ers reportedly land DeForest Buckner for fourth-round pick in trade with Colts
headlines.description: The 49ers reunited with a familiar face. San Francisco acquired three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner in a trade with the Indianapolis Colts, NFL Media’s Ian Rapoport reported Tuesday. Rapoport also reported that the 49ers are sending the Colts a 2027 fourth-round draft pick in the deal. The 32-year-old Buckner, who San Francisco selected with the No. 7 pick in the 2016 NFL Draft, spent the first four seasons of his NFL career with the 49ers, where he was selected to a Pro Bowl in 2018 before he was traded to Indianapolis for a first-round pick in the 2020 NFL Draft that became defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw. In seven games with the Colts this season, Buckner has 31 combined tackles (11 solo, 20 assisted), four tackles for loss, eight quarterback hits, three passes defensed, one fumble recovery and four sacks. Buckner originally signed a two-year, $46 million contract extension with Indianapolis in April of 2024, and has a $7.9 million salary cap hit this season before he is set to become an unrestricted free agent this upcoming offseason. The 49ers’ defensive line has held up admirably this season in defensive end Nick Bosa’s absence, but another solid pass-rusher and run-stopper like Buckner certainly can elevate the unit as a whole. Now heading into their Week 8 bye, San Francisco will have plenty of time to get Buckner acclimated to new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris’ system before the Week 9 game vs. the Las Vegas Raiders at Levi’s Stadium. headlines.title: High tide flooding causes road closures in Mill Valley
headlines.description: Two roads are closed due to flooding in Mill Valley on Tuesday, according to an advisory issued by police. Mill Valley police issued an alert around noontime advising drivers to avoid Miller Avenue between Camino Alto and Almonte Boulevard. That is the section that runs between Tamalpais High School and the Bothin Marsh Preserve. Also closed is the west side of Redwood Highway, also called Frontage Road, between Hamilton Drive and the on ramp for southbound Highway 101. The road closures require traffic to detour until the flooding recedes. The National Weather Service has issued a Coastal Flood Advisory that will be in effect through 5 p.m. Friday for bayshore locations along San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay, as well as low-lying areas along the Pacific Coast.

headlines.title: Preliminary 2.6 magnitude earthquake strikes near San Jose
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.6 magnitude earthquake struck near San Jose Tuesday afternoon, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 12:38 p.m. and was centered 9 miles east of Seven Trees, 9 miles east-southeast of Alum Rock and 9.8 miles east of Communications Hill, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Risks spelled out for Anthropic investors include blowback from runaway AI
headlines.description: Any time a company looks to start selling shares on Wall Street, it’s required to disclose potential risks to investors. In the case of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic, that has included the possibility that its products could threaten nothing less than humanity itself. The risks laid out by the San Francisco company in its filing Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission included discussion of bad actors potentially using AI models to build deadly weapons or the technology itself going rogue with untold consequences. Of the 335 pages outlining Anthropic’s finances, executive compensation, dividend policy and the like, 93 pages are devoted to “risk factors” — the things that could hurt potential shareholders’ investments. Rival SpaceX’s listed risk factors, in comparison, took up 38 out of more than 250 pages. In selling itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses. “To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” wrote the company’s founders in a letter to prospective shareholders in the IPO filing. “Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organization, founded in large part to help the world realize AI’s benefits and avoid its dangers.” The technology’s potential benefits include leaps in curing diseases and productivity boosts across every sector of the economy, the company said. Still, the potential liabilities are many. They range from the mundane — the possibility it won’t be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation. Here is a look at some of the risks Anthropic details: The technology’s rapid development Anthropic said it’s possible its models could develop so quickly the company won’t be able to implement adequate safety measures, “which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in September that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet. The warning — and now Anthropic’s move to sell shares — comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also act on their own to carry out other, more harmful tasks. As AI systems “become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the SEC filing said, there’s a risk that such systems could “take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” “Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business,” Anthropic said. Now that the AI models are themselves contributing to Anthropic’s own research and development, it’s possible that AI could progress “beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models,” according to the filing. This, the document said, could adversely affect Anthropic’s business. Malicious actors could cause mayhem with the technology The filing discussed concerns that advanced AI systems, if not developed and operated with enough safeguards and oversight, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.” The company said it would be harmed if use by bad actors causes damage, “or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse.” Anthropic sketched out the prospect of bad actors using AI models to build chemical weapons or authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens. In September, the company disclosed that it had blocked efforts to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapon development. The company could run up against limits on processing powe r Compute — the computing power or resources needed to build, test and improve AI models — is expensive and in high demand. Anthropic notes that if it’s unable to secure adequate compute, or if “we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.” Anthropic mentioned community opposition to data centers as a risk to its business. Data center development “has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources,” the filing said, adding that if regulators impose new requirements or charges as a result, its ability to do business could suffer. In addition, the company relies on a small number of customers, including SpaceX and Microsoft, and distribution channels for a large portion of its revenue. This means that even if just one of its big customers decides to scale back — or drop the company altogether — Anthropic said it could see its prospects and finances suffer. Mitigating the risks In some ways, AI’s enormous risk, combined with its enormous potential, is Anthropic’s main selling point. The company has tried to position itself as a responsible AI company, and courts business customers by emphasizing safety-mindedness. “We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology,” the filing said. Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Research, said IPO deals have to display “very clearly” what risks people face when they invest their money in a newly public stock. “One of the things that’s great about our capital markets here domestically is the level of transparency that you must commit to, to be a publicly traded corporation on a U.S. exchange requires you to outline those risks in a very clear way, so that people understand if they want to participate by offering their hard-earned money and help finance this type of a deal,” he said. ___ AP Business Writer Bernard Condon and AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed to this story.

headlines.title: Watch: Great white shark cruises by kayak fisherman off Half Moon Bay
headlines.description: David Slavich has spent years enjoying the ocean, but a close encounter with a great white shark near Half Moon Bay last weekend was unlike anything he’s ever experienced out on the water. Slavich was fishing from his kayak on Sunday when the shark approached from behind. “I heard this little splash behind my shoulder,” Slavich told NBC Bay Area. “I look back and I just see this massive fin and shadow. This thing is bigger than my kayak. My kayak’s 12 and a half feet. This thing dwarfed it. Just panic set in.” A camera attached to Slavich captured the entire encounter. “Oh my God. There’s a great white shark,” Slavich can be heard saying. Slavich then repeated “Oh my God” several times as the shark slowly cruised by along the surface of the water. “It was absolutely frightening,” Slavich said. “I think the scariest thing that’s every happened to me in my entire life.” Monterey County Oct 26 Monterey County Oct 19 Despite the scare, Slavich said he stayed out on the water and continued to fish for another three to four hours. “I think like a lot of folks that spend time out on the water here in Northern California or California in general, the boogeyman is the great white shark,” he said. “When you’re surfing, spearfishing, out in the water, it’s just sort of in the back of your mind all the time. Every splash or seagull or anything while I’m out there, I’m hyperaware.” Slavich said he’ll plan to use the buddy system when he heads out on his next ocean adventure. “I need to go with a buddy,” he said. “That’s the safest way to go. I’m not solo kayaking out there any more. That’s one thing I’ll change for sure.”

headlines.title: FBI agent cross-examined in Sheng Thao corruption trial
headlines.description: An FBI agent who investigated former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao for alleged corruption is back on the stand Tuesday in Oakland federal court. This time, FBI Special Agent Katherine Barclay is being questioned by the attorney for Andre Jones, Thao’s longtime partner. Jones’ attorney tried to show the jury Tuesday morning that Jones was not involved in a corruption and bribery scheme to get Thao elected mayor. During cross-examination, Barclay testified that Jones didn’t respond to a number of texts from businessman Mario Juarez asking for Jones’ thoughts on a negative campaign mailer against Loren Taylor, who ran against Thao. Juarez has pleaded guilty for his role in the alleged scheme, which included producing the mailers in return for favors from Thao when elected mayor. When Jones finally responded to the text, he said that if he helped with the mailer, it would be “coordinating” and that Juarez should run it by someone else. Barclay also testified there are no recorded phone calls with Juarez, which the defense argues is proof Jones didn’t conspire with Juarez. Juarez is expected to testify later on behalf of the prosecution in exchange for a lighter sentence. Prosecutors allege Thao, Jones and David and Andy Duong were part of a bribery and corruption scheme to help Thao get elected and siphon money to Jones in exchange for favors to the Duong family, which owns California Waste Solutions, Oakland’s recycling contractor. headlines.title: Man reaches the Bay Area after walking across the country from New York City
headlines.description: Before this summer, Chantz Rivera, 29, had left his hometown in New York City twice in his life. On May 31, Rivera headed out of the Bronx on foot, starting a long-planned walk across the country. On Monday, nearly five months later, he touched Bay Area waters for the first time. “I rolled my pants up,” said Rivera in a phone interview from a bike path in Mill Valley on Monday. “The water’s kinda clear, lowkey.” Thanks to recent El Niño storms, the path had flooded, with water from the Bay almost reaching Highway 101. Rivera had to push his cart of belongings through a few inches of seawater. “I feel great,” he said, surprising himself. He arrived in the Bay Area almost two months ahead of schedule. Since setting out, Rivera has camped beside highways, gazed up at the Rocky Mountains, watched bighorn sheep graze, eaten home-cooked meals in Kansas and gotten a handful of free motel stays along the way from generous strangers. “I want to do it just to be free, not to be stuck,” said Rivera. “To experience life more, adventure more, you got to break out of your comfort zone.” Rivera grew up in Gun Hill Houses, a public housing project in the Bronx. Up to now, he had only ever traveled to Washington, D.C., and Florida for brief trips. Before his trek across America, Rivera was working warehouse jobs around New York City and long stints as a dishwasher. One of his fears, he said, was being trapped in routine. So, he decided to take a walk. Rivera stuck mostly to U.S. Routes 40 and 50 through New Jersey, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Colorado, Utah, Nevada and now California. To keep him going, he said, he listened to music. Three rappers specifically have been on rotation: Lil Durk, A Boogie Wit da Hoodie and Future. Rivera started his trip with just $250, he said. Along the way, people have asked how they could support him, so he went ahead and put together A GoFundMe campaign in August. As of Monday, Rivera raised over $13,000. In his journey, Rivera said he was surprised to learn that so many strangers were moved by something that started out as a personal goal. “I was really doing it for me to not be stuck,” said Rivera. “I get a great feeling that it’s inspiring people. I’m grateful.” For the next week, Rivera said he plans to just relax and explore San Francisco before heading to do the same in Los Angeles. He hopes to be back in the Bronx by Thanksgiving — this time traveling by airplane.

headlines.title: Crash blocked northbound lanes of Golden Gate Bridge
headlines.description: The northbound lanes of the Golden Gate Bridge were blocked following a crash Tuesday morning, according to the California Highway Patrol. The crash was reported shortly after 6 a.m. and blocked traffic for more than an hour. The San Francisco Department of Emergency Management warned people to expect delays and use alternate routes if possible.

headlines.title: San Jose City Council to vote on new name for downtown plaza
headlines.description: The San Jose City Council is expected to finalize the renaming of what was once Plaza de Cesar Chavez on Tuesday. The city covered the late labor leader’s name and removed the memorial plaque after serious and credible allegations of sexual abuse and assault were made against him. Since then, the city has worked with stakeholders to find a more appropriate way to honor the labor movement rather than one of the people behind it. After several community events and a public survey, two favorites emerged and will be combined as the final recommendation. On Tuesday, the City Council will vote on whether to approve “Plaza del Pueblo de San Jose” as the new and permanent name of the downtown landmark. People in San Jose submitted more than 600 name suggestions, and the naming survey drew more than 10,000 responses. San Jose Aug 25 San Jose Jun 24 San Jose launches effort to rename former Cesar Chavez plaza

headlines.title: Conservationists celebrate sighting of North American river otter on San Mateo coast
headlines.description: Conservationists are celebrating after a North American river otter was sighted recently along the San Mateo coast for the first time in more than 100 years. The otter was photographed by wildlife cameras within a closed area of the Cloverdale Ranch Open Space Preserve in Pescadero in July, August and September. The cameras were set up to photograph other animals, such as foxes, so it was a welcome surprise when a river otter made an appearance, according to the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District. “Checking wildlife cameras can be like Christmas, but river otters haven’t been known to occur on the San Mateo Coast since the 1800s,” said Ken Hickman, an independent researcher and Midpen partner. “I knew Midpen and State Parks biologists would be as surprised and interested as I was to see the photos.” The river otter species Lontra canadensis once ranged along the west coast of North America, from Alaska down to Santa Barbara County, but the 19th-century fur trade and pollution decimated their populations. There has been a resurgence of the otters north of the Golden Gate and some appearances in the San Francisco Bay wetlands, but virtually no sightings along the Pacific Coast. Because river otters thrive in clean water with abundant food supplies, the sighting has ecological significance, according to Midpen officials. “River otters can serve as vital bioindicators,” said Midpen biologist Matt Sharp Chaney. “Their presence in Cloverdale Ranch Preserve and the reclamation of their historic range offers evidence of the species’ recovery post-fur trade in protected resilient landscapes that also support coho salmon and steelhead trout.” Representatives of the River Otter Ecology Project were also celebrating the sighting. “This discovery suggests that what we have long expected is happening: river otters are making their way to excellent habitat along the San Mateo coast,” said Megan Isadore, executive director of River Otter Ecology Project. “It reminds us that people have the knowledge and ability to protect and restore the habitats that allow river otters, and many other species, to recover,” Isadore said. “We must continue to support that recovery.” The River Otter Ecology Project encourages the public to submit river otter observations to Otter Spotter, its community science observations platform at riverotterecology.org.

headlines.title: California joins FTC lawsuit accusing Dollar General of overcharging customers
headlines.description: The Federal Trade Commission has sued the bargain chain Dollar General for what it characterized as “long-running deceptive pricing practices” by charging customers more once they reach the register than the prices that are displayed on shelves and in advertisements. Twenty states, including California, joined in the complaint, filed by the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. It said that Dollar General, which operates 21,000 stores nationwide, failed to correct the issue despite what it said was “extensive corporate knowledge of the problem.” “Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” wrote Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. One of the issues, according to the agency, is understaffing. Although Dollar General has policies in place to align register prices with shelf prices based on guidance from corporate, thinly staffed stores lack the time to meet these demands. It says executives at the company are aware of the issue, citing internal communications. “For example, in a news article sent to the CEO of the company and others, a former assistant manager in Illinois stated that she spent many of her shifts as the only person working in her store: ‘You’re lucky if you get to work two to four hours of your eight-to 13-hour shift with another human being.'” Dollar General, based in Goodlettsville, Tennessee, just outside of Nashville, did not respond to a request for comment, but pushed back against the allegations in a statement posted on its website. The company said the lawsuit suggests they “abandoned our mission and willfully disregarded the affordability needs of our customers. Nothing could be further from the truth.” “Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store. As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement,” the company said. However, the FTC noted dozens of examples in the 95-page lawsuit of employees at stores around the country denying customers price corrections. In one example from earlier this year, a Texas customer said when he complained about being overcharged from the advertised price, the employee reportedly told him “I have to overcharge you or I will get in trouble!!!!” “In November 2025, a Florida consumer complained about being charged $2.50 for a bottle of Johnson & Johnson baby shampoo when the price on the shelf was $2.00. When this consumer raised the issue with the store employee, the employee gave the consumer the option of paying the higher price or not purchasing the baby shampoo,” according to the lawsuit. The states joining the FTC lawsuit include: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin, according to the FTC.
